name: libsecp256k1 (bitcoin-core/secp256k1)
workload: ECDSA signature verification on the secp256k1 curve: parse a compressed pubkey and DER-encoded signature, then verify, over many pseudo-random (pubkey, msghash, signature) triplets; run across every historical release of OpenSSL (0.9.8h-3.5.0) and libsecp256k1 via dlopen-based dynamic loading
claimed_speedup: libsecp256k1 (latest release) is more than 8x faster than OpenSSL (latest release) for ECDSA verification on secp256k1; independently reproduced at a ratio of 8.5x on an AMD Ryzen 5950X (500000 iterations)
compiler_and_flags: gcc 14.2.0; default shared-library builds (OpenSSL: ./config shared && make; libsecp256k1: default build), no special optimization flags beyond upstream defaults
hardware: author's arm64 machine (3 machines tested with similar results); independently reproduced on an AMD Ryzen 5950X by libsecp256k1 author Pieter Wuille
stars_or_usage: 2.5k+ stars; the ECDSA/Schnorr library used by Bitcoin Core, Ethereum, and most secp256k1 signing/verification worldwide
tradeoffs: libsecp256k1 is narrowly scoped to secp256k1 (and a few related curves), trading OpenSSL's broad general-purpose API surface for curve-specific speed (GLV endomorphism, safegcd modular inverse)
caveats: Benchmark builds libsecp256k1 with default settings only, not Bitcoin Core's specific compile-time configuration, so the real-world gap in Bitcoin Core may differ; author explicitly cautions this is not evidence OpenSSL's EC code is slow in general, since OpenSSL's secp256r1 path is heavily optimized and secp256k1 is a low priority for OpenSSL outside Bitcoin
found_via: gh search code "faster than OpenSSL" signature -> jamesob/delving-bitcoin-archive rendered transcript of a delvingbitcoin.org forum/blog post by theStack (Nov 2025), benchmark code at github.com/theStack/secp256k1-plugbench

name: Snowshoe (catid/snowshoe)
workload: Elliptic-curve scalar multiplication / EC-DH and signature-style operations (ec_mul, ec_simul) on a custom ~252-bit curve at ~128-bit security, cycle-counted with RDTSC (Turbo Boost disabled), compared against OpenSSL 1.0.1e's P-256 timing tests and a third-party paper's OpenSSL-optimization results
claimed_speedup: author states Snowshoe is 'roughly 6x faster than OpenSSL 1.0.1e for the same security level'; own OpenSSL 1.0.1e make-tests run showed ~4x slower key generation and ~8x slower EC-DH than Snowshoe (derived from page data)
hardware: Sandy Bridge / Ivy Bridge era Intel CPUs (Core i5-2557M, i7-2600, i7-3770), Turbo Boost disabled, RDTSC cycle counts
tradeoffs: Targets a custom non-standard curve rather than NIST P-256 or secp256k1, limiting interoperability; project is explicitly pre-1.0/experimental
caveats: OpenSSL baseline (1.0.1e, 2013) is over a decade out of date; the 6x figure combines the author's own cycle counts with a separate paper's (Kasper) OpenSSL optimization results via derived arithmetic rather than a single direct head-to-head run; capped at tier C for outdated/indirect baseline per hard rules
found_via: gh search code "x faster" "signature verification" -> catid/snowshoe README Benchmarks section

name: Dilithium-AVX512 (companion code for 'Optimized Vectorization Implementation of CRYSTALS-Dilithium')
baseline: CRYSTALS-Dilithium AVX2 reference implementation (pq-crystals/dilithium, the implementation liboqs wraps)
workload: Dilithium2/3/5 key generation, signing, and verification, cycle-counted; fully vectorized AVX-512 implementation (tailored PSPM-TEE small-polynomial multiplication, AVX-512IFMA-based reduction) benchmarked against the authors' own AVX2 implementation of the same operations
claimed_speedup: AVX-512 implementation is 43.2%/39.3%/45.6% faster at key generation, 36.6%/41.6%/43.7% faster at signing, and 45.3%/46.5%/47.4% faster at verification for Dilithium2/3/5 respectively vs. their AVX2 baseline; the underlying PSPM-TEE multiplication is 47%-66% faster than NTT-based multiplication
compiler_and_flags: gcc, -O3 -march=native -mtune=native, targeting AVX-512F/BW/CD/VL/DQ plus AVX2 (per repo Makefile)
hardware: Intel x86-64 CPU platform (exact CPU model not stated in the paper or repo)
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 (including the IFMA subset) for full benefit, narrowing deployable hardware versus a portable AVX2/reference build; implementation has not been independently audited
caveats: Repo has no LICENSE file, so it is reference/study-only, not a permissively licensed drop-in; comparison baseline is the authors' own AVX2 build rather than a named liboqs or OpenSSL release, and exact CPU model is never disclosed, capping evidence at tier C
found_via: gh search code PSPM-TEE (surfaced xurq5953 fork, already in KNOWN_LIST) traced to arXiv paper 2306.01989 'Optimized Vectorization Implementation of CRYSTALS-Dilithium'; located its companion code repo Dilithium-AVX512/Dilithium-AVX512
